title: 0/1 knapsack: subset enumeration vs meet in the middle vs pseudo-polynomial DP
problem_statement: Given n items with positive integer weights w_i and values v_i and an integer capacity W, compute the maximum total value of a subset whose total weight is at most W.

input.size_measure: Theta(n log(max value) + n log(max weight) + log W) bits. W is a number, so the input contains only log W bits for it.

algorithms.name: subset enumeration
algorithms.pseudocode: for each subset S: if w(S) <= W: best = max(best, v(S))

algorithms.name: meet in the middle (Horowitz-Sahni)
algorithms.idea: Split the items into halves, enumerate the 2^(n/2) subsets of each, sort one half by weight with a running maximum of value, and binary-search the best partner for every subset of the other half.
algorithms.correctness: Every subset is a union of a left subset and a right subset; for a fixed left subset the best right partner is the most valuable one of weight <= W - w(left), which the prefix maximum over the weight-sorted list returns (Horowitz & Sahni 1974).

algorithms.name: capacity DP (Bellman)
algorithms.idea: best[c] = max value achievable with capacity c, updated item by item in decreasing c so each item is used at most once.
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n W): pseudo-polynomial (polynomial in the VALUE W, exponential in its bit length)
algorithms.correctness: Standard DP; optimal substructure over (item prefix, capacity).

relationship: Enumeration Theta(2^n n) -> meet in the middle Theta(2^(n/2) n): a verified exponential-to-better-exponential improvement (T8). The DP Theta(nW) beats both whenever W << 2^(n/2), but it is NOT polynomial in the input size: adding one bit to W adds one bit to the input yet doubles the DP's running time. No algorithm polynomial in the input size is known; 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard (Karp 1972), so one would imply P = NP.

sources.title: Reducibility among combinatorial problems
sources.venue: Complexity of Computer Computations, Plenum Press, 85-103

sources.title: Computing partitions with applications to the knapsack problem
sources.note: Meet-in-the-middle O(2^(n/2) n): an exponential-to-better-exponential improvement.

sources.authors: Ibarra, O. H.; Kim, C. E.
sources.title: Fast approximation algorithms for the knapsack and sum of subset problems
sources.note: FPTAS: (1 - eps)-approximation in time polynomial in n and 1/eps.

verification.method: V1: all three agree on random instances (weights 1..20, values 1..30, capacity = half the total weight; enumeration up to n = 14, the others up to n = 24) and respect an independent greedy lower bound. V2: runtimes fitted against 2^n n, 2^(n/2) n and n^2. The DP's n^2 is specific to this harness: weights are bounded, so W = Theta(n) and Theta(nW) = Theta(n^2). The fit says nothing about large W, which is the pseudo-polynomial case.

caveats: Cautionary entry (START_HERE section 4): pseudo-polynomial is not polynomial. Primary T6 because a polynomial algorithm in the input size is open (and implies P = NP); secondary T8 for enumeration -> meet in the middle. The DP is recorded for its teaching value, not as a pair.
notes: Good teaching case for the input-size definition in START_HERE section 1.
